groups.instructions: Read the report about birds using school courtyards and answer the questions.
groups.passage:
For a geography project, students compared bird activity in two courtyards. The east courtyard contained three trees and a narrow garden bed. The west courtyard had one tree and more benches. After five mornings, the east courtyard had more recorded visits. The group wrote that birds preferred sites with more trees.

A groundskeeper pointed out a detail they had overlooked. The east courtyard was visible from a second-floor window, where most of the counting had been done. Students had watched the west courtyard from a doorway, and a nearby wall blocked their view of part of the roof. The comparison treated an unobserved visit as if it had never happened. The team arranged for pairs to use first-floor windows with views of roughly the same area in both courtyards. They also agreed to count for the same length of time just before the first lesson.

On the new sheets, the difference between courtyards was smaller. The students also noted that visits were more common on mornings when building doors stayed closed until the first bell. On other mornings, pupils crossed both courtyards on the way to club meetings. The team could not tell whether movement, sound or something else linked to those meetings explained the pattern.

Instead of naming a preferred courtyard, the final report recommended improving the observations. It suggested taking notes during quiet and busy periods in each courtyard. It also separated sightings of a bird on the ground from sightings of one flying overhead. A tree might matter to a bird that stops to rest, while a bird passing above both courtyards might give little information about either.

questions.question_text: What did the students initially conclude after five mornings?

options.text: Birds preferred sites with more trees.
The west courtyard had fewer usable benches.
The two courtyards received an equal number of visits.
Birds were more active after the first lesson.

questions.question_text: How could the wall have affected the original result?

options.text: It made the entire east courtyard noisier.
It could hide part of the west courtyard area from observers.
It gave birds a direct route to the east courtyard.
It prevented students from standing by the east window.

questions.question_text: What does “they” refer to in “a detail they had overlooked”?

options.text: The students carrying out the comparison.
The birds counted from the window.
The people maintaining the school buildings.
The pupils attending morning club meetings.

questions.question_text: Which change most directly addressed the problem raised by the groundskeeper?

options.text: Starting the next round before the first lesson.
Writing the findings into a geography report.
Telling pupils to enter for club meetings quietly.
Using vantage points that revealed comparable areas.

questions.question_text: What happened to the recorded gap between the courtyards in the second round?

options.text: It disappeared from the sheets because dates were missing.
It shifted mainly to observations during the first lesson.

questions.question_text: Why did the students avoid claiming that footsteps caused the pattern?

options.text: They did not know which mornings had club meetings.
They had not separated movement from other conditions linked to club mornings.
They had found no relationship between visits and the state of the doors.
They had observed that all birds were flying far above the roofs.

questions.question_text: Why separate ground sightings from birds seen overhead?

options.text: Birds overhead are easier to count than all the birds near trees.
A bird on the ground cannot be seen from any upper window.
Flying birds show a more reliable preference for the courtyard with more trees.
A bird using the courtyard offers stronger evidence about the site than one merely passing by.

questions.question_text: Which additional procedure best fits the final report?

options.text: Compare a busy period at one site with a quiet period at the other.
Record only total visits and pool sightings from ground and sky.
Observe both sites during matched quiet periods and matched busy periods.
Drop all visits on quiet days to match the club schedule.

questions.question_text: What is the report mainly about?

options.text: Checking how many trees a school can plant near its buildings.
Improving observation methods before claiming that birds favour one of two sites.
Choosing a morning when pupils can safely watch birds from the roof.
Explaining why all birds prefer gardens with plenty of trees.

groups.instructions: Read the essay about placing outdoor sculpture and answer the questions.
groups.passage:
A town bought a long stone sculpture for a new square. In the artist's studio, it had looked like two low waves viewed from the front. The town initially put it in the centre of the square and left a clear area all around. At lunchtime, people rarely stood in the intended viewing spot. Most approached from a narrow side street, where the two forms lined up and looked like a single block. Some leaned bicycles against it without noticing the gap between the forms.

The artist could have asked for barriers to keep people in the intended position. Instead, she spent two afternoons watching where they entered and where they paused. A low wall near a row of trees turned out to be a regular meeting place. From there the sculpture had more depth, but a rubbish bin blocked one end. The town moved the bin, tried rotating the sculpture slightly and left the work in the same broad area for a month. Walkers approaching from the side street could then see a gap much sooner.

Some councillors still wondered why the work could not be moved beside a lake, where there was a longer uninterrupted view. A landscape designer explained that the square was not simply a place to display the sculpture. The two stone forms also marked the transition from the busy side street to a wider area where people slowed down. At the lake, the distant view might be clearer, but the work would no longer have that relationship to a daily route.

The final plan retained ordinary uses of the square. People could still wait by the wall, and two bicycle stands were added close to the side street. Nobody was asked to follow a prescribed path. The artist said she had learned to judge the piece at the speed of someone walking to lunch, not only at the speed of a visitor who had come especially to study it.

questions.question_text: How did the sculpture appear to many people arriving from the side street at first?

options.text: The two forms appeared to merge into one block.
The gap looked wider than it had in the studio.
The forms looked like three separate waves.
The forms were hidden entirely behind a low wall.

questions.question_text: What does the detail about bicycles help illustrate?

options.text: The square was originally designed mainly for a bicycle race.
Cyclists were the only group able to see the gap.
Some users treated the stone as a practical object and overlooked part of its shape.
The sculpture was placed in an existing bike rack.

questions.question_text: What does “intended” mean in “the intended viewing spot”?
Which place turned out to be a common meeting point?

options.text: The centre of the side street.
A low wall by a row of trees.

questions.question_text: Which two changes did the town make before leaving the work in place for a month?

options.text: Moving the rubbish bin and turning the sculpture slightly.
Removing the wall and resurfacing the side street.
Putting barriers around the work and blocking the square.
Moving the artwork beside a lake and planting trees at its old site.

questions.question_text: Why did the artist observe people's movement before altering the arrangement?

options.text: She needed to prove nobody was using the square during the day.
She hoped people would suggest new materials for the stone forms.
She was deciding whether to ask visitors to pay for a guided route.
She wanted changes that worked with familiar routes and stopping points.

questions.question_text: What advantage did the lake have in the councillors' proposal?

options.text: It offered a longer open view of the sculpture.
More people passed it daily on their way to lunch.
The low wall there was already a common meeting spot.
Its paths made the sculpture mark the change from a narrow street to a square.

questions.question_text: What would be lost by moving the sculpture to the lake, according to the designer?

options.text: The artist's ability to display both stone forms together.
Its role in marking a change along people's everyday route.
The opportunity to look at it from far away.
The town's permission to use the stone outdoors.

questions.question_text: In paragraph three, what would no longer have the same relationship to a daily route?
Which option best expresses the artist's lesson in the final sentence?

options.text: Judge how the work appears to people passing through on their daily routes as well as to people who come to look closely.
Ask visitors to slow down so that everyone can inspect the work at the same speed.
Let daily users decide on the price before commissioning future art.
Design sculptures to be understood only by visitors who deliberately seek them out.

questions.question_text: Which title best fits this essay?

options.text: How Stone Waves Are Carved in a Workshop.
Placing Public Art Where Everyday Life Happens.
The Town Square That Banned Bicycles.
Why Sculptures Always Need an Empty Background.
